claim: Microtubules (MTs) are key components of the cytoskeleton and play a central role in cell division and development.
source: Microtubules (MTs) are key components of the cytoskeleton and play a central role in cell division and development.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell biology supported by the citation (Hyams and Lloyd, 1994) in the full text.

claim: MT assembly is known to be associated with a structural change in αβ-tubulin dimers from kinked to straight conformations.
source: MT assembly is known to be associated with a structural change in αβ-tubulin dimers from kinked to straight conformations.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to structural studies cited in the Introduction section.

claim: GTP-tubulin favors a broad range of almost isoenergetic curvatures.
source: Contrary to existing allosteric and lattice models, we find that GTP-tubulin favors a broad range of almost isoenergetic curvatures, whereas GDP-tubulin has a much lower bending flexibility.
evidence: This claim is supported by free energy calculations shown in Figure 6, which demonstrate that GTP-tubulin samples a wider range of curvatures with similar free energy values.

claim: GDP-tubulin has a much lower bending flexibility compared to GTP-tubulin.
source: Contrary to existing allosteric and lattice models, we find that GTP-tubulin favors a broad range of almost isoenergetic curvatures, whereas GDP-tubulin has a much lower bending flexibility.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the steeper free energy curves for GDP-tubulin in Figure 6 compared to GTP-tubulin.

claim: Two conformational states exist differing in location of the anchor point connecting the monomers that affects tubulin bending.
source: Moreover, irrespective of the bound nucleotide and curvature, two conformational states exist differing in location of the anchor point connecting the monomers that affects tubulin bending, with one state being strongly favored in solution.
evidence: This is supported by the ensemble separation analysis shown in Figure 4 and Figure 7, which identify two distinct free energy basins.

claim: One anchor point state is strongly favored in solution.
source: Moreover, irrespective of the bound nucleotide and curvature, two conformational states exist differing in location of the anchor point connecting the monomers that affects tubulin bending, with one state being strongly favored in solution.
evidence: The free energy difference between the two states is estimated to be ΔΔG_TB-SB = 8.6 ± 2.4 kT, indicating that the SB state is strongly favored (~99.98% population).

claim: MTs stochastically switch between growing and shrinking phases even under sufficient free tubulin concentrations.
source: Unlike other cytoskeletal components in the cell, for example, actin filaments which continuously grow as long as enough G-actin is present, MTs stochastically switch between growing and shrinking phases even under sufficient free tubulin concentrations.
evidence: This is a well-documented phenomenon known as dynamic instability, supported by citations (Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984; Gardner et al., 2011).

claim: Free tubulin requires guanosine triphosphate (GTP) to initiate the formation of new MTs (nucleation) and elongate already existing ones (growth).
source: Free tubulin requires guanosine triphosphate (GTP) to initiate the formation of new MTs (nucleation) and elongate already existing ones (growth) (Weisenberg et al., 1968; Weisenberg, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations cited in the text.

claim: GTP-tubulin stacks head-to-tail at the tips of growing MTs and forms one-dimensional protofilaments that associate laterally to create a hollow cylinder typically comprising 13–14 protofilaments.
source: In the latter case, GTP-tubulin stacks head-to-tail at the tips of growing MTs (primarily those capped by β-tubulin) and forms one-dimensional protofilaments that associate laterally to create a hollow cylinder typically comprising 13–14 protofilaments.
evidence: This describes the structural organization of microtubules based on established knowledge.

claim: Every tubulin dimer contains two GTP-binding sites: one nonexchangeable site buried in the intradimer contact and one exchangeable site exposed on the outer surface of the β-subunit.
source: Every dimer contains two GTP-binding sites: one nonexchangeable site that is buried in the intradimer contact and one exchangeable site exposed on the outer surface of the β-subunit.
evidence: This is a well-established structural feature of tubulin dimers.

claim: Upon addition of a tubulin dimer to a growing MT end, α-tubulin in the incoming dimer completes the GTP-binding pocket of β-tubulin in the preceding dimer, which enables the hydrolysis of GTP.
source: Upon addition of a tubulin dimer to a growing MT end, α-tubulin in the incoming dimer completes the GTP-binding pocket of β-tubulin in the preceding dimer, which enables the hydrolysis of GTP in the pocket, i.e. cleavage of GTP into a guanosine diphosphate (GDP) and a γ-phosphate.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of GTP hydrolysis in the MT lattice based on structural understanding.

claim: MTs grow steadily as long as GTP hydrolysis in the lattice lags behind the arrival of new dimers, which creates the so-called GTP cap at the MT tip.
source: MTs grow steadily as long as GTP hydrolysis in the lattice lags behind the arrival of new dimers, which creates the so-called GTP cap at the MT tip (Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984).
evidence: This is the GTP cap model of MT dynamic instability, supported by citation.

claim: If a MT occasionally grows at a slower rate than GTP hydrolysis, the MT lattice depolymerizes rapidly.
source: If a MT occasionally grows at a slower rate than GTP hydrolysis, the MT lattice depolymerizes rapidly.
evidence: This describes the catastrophe event in MT dynamic instability.

claim: Tubulin dimers are straight when locked in the MT lattice.
source: Analysis of electron microscopy images of MTs and structural data have revealed that tubulin dimers are straight when locked in the MT lattice (Nogales et al., 1998; Li et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by structural studies cited in the text.

claim: Tubulin straightening takes place during polymerization.
source: It has hence become clear that tubulin straightening takes place during polymerization, whereas strongly kinked conformations are characteristic of depolymerized GDP-tubulin.
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations of tubulin in different polymerization states.

claim: Strongly kinked conformations are characteristic of depolymerized GDP-tubulin.
source: It has hence become clear that tubulin straightening takes place during polymerization, whereas strongly kinked conformations are characteristic of depolymerized GDP-tubulin.
evidence: This is based on structural observations of GDP-tubulin.

claim: The allosteric model postulates an equilibrium between two conformations of free tubulin, straight and kinked, under the allosteric control of the nucleotide state.
source: According to the allosteric model (Figure 1, right branch), there is an equilibrium between two conformations of free tubulin, straight and kinked, under the allosteric control of the nucleotide state.
evidence: This describes one of the two canonical models of MT assembly discussed in the literature.

claim: In the allosteric model, free tubulin dimers bind GTP prior to assembly, which triggers a kinked-to-straight conformational change.
source: Here, free tubulin dimers bind GTP prior to assembly, which triggers a kinked-to-straight conformational change such that dimer integration into the MT lattice is sterically compatible.
evidence: This describes the mechanism proposed by the allosteric model.

claim: The allosteric model has been supported by the observation of an intermediate curvature state of tubulin at low temperatures using a nonhydrolyzable GTP analog.
source: This model has been supported by the observation of an intermediate curvature state of tubulin at low temperatures using a nonhydrolyzable GTP analog (Müller-Reichert et al., 1998; Wang and Nogales, 2005).
evidence: This cites experimental evidence supporting the allosteric model.

claim: The lattice model postulates that free tubulin adopts a kinked conformation in solution irrespectively of the nucleotide state.
source: Alternatively, the lattice model (Figure 1, left branch) postulates that free tubulin adopts a kinked conformation in solution irrespectively of the nucleotide state, and only upon integration into the MT lattice, tubulin dimers are forced into a straight conformation.
evidence: This describes the alternative canonical model of MT assembly.

claim: In the lattice model, the role of GTP binding is not to control the intrinsic tubulin conformation but to strengthen the dimer-dimer bonds in the lattice.
source: Here, the role of GTP binding is not to control the intrinsic tubulin conformation but to strengthen the dimer-dimer bonds in the lattice.
evidence: This describes the mechanism proposed by the lattice model.

claim: The lattice model relies on observations from MT drug binding assays and small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) experiments.
source: This model relies on observations from MT drug binding assays and small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) experiments (Manuel Andreu et al., 1989; Buey et al., 2006; Rice et al., 2008).
evidence: This cites experimental evidence supporting the lattice model.

claim: Crystal structures of unassembled tubulin in all relevant nucleotide states did not show marked differences between the different nucleotide states, thus supporting the lattice model.
source: These structures did not show marked differences between the different nucleotide states, thus supporting the lattice model.
evidence: This is based on structural studies cited in the text (Gigant et al., 2005; Nawrotek et al., 2011; Ayaz et al., 2012; Prota et al., 2013).

claim: MD simulations of both GTP- and GDP-tubulin in solution for several tens of nanoseconds found both to be kinked.
source: The intrinsic conformational dynamics of both GTP- and GDP-tubulin in solution have also been simulated for several tens of nanoseconds using all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) and both were found to be kinked (Gebremichael et al., 2008).
evidence: This cites previous computational studies.

claim: Longer MD simulations (up to 100 ns) have not revealed GTP-induced tubulin straightening.
source: Longer MD simulations (up to 100 ns) have not revealed GTP-induced tubulin straightening either (Bennett et al., 2009; Grafmüller and Voth, 2011; André et al., 2012; Grafmüller et al., 2013).
evidence: This cites previous computational studies.

claim: Lateral binding of two GDP-tubulin dimers has been shown to shift the conformations of individual dimers toward the straight state.
source: In another computational study, lateral binding of two GDP-tubulin dimers has been shown to shift the conformations of individual dimers toward the straight state; the GTP-state was not analyzed though (Peng et al., 2014).
evidence: This cites a previous computational study.

claim: Two β-tubulin mutations (D417H and R262H) related to ocular motility disorder in humans substantially affect MT dynamics.
source: Recently, the allosteric model has been supported by tubulin polymerization assays and structural experiments which showed that two β-tubulin mutations (D417H and R262H) related to ocular motility disorder in humans substantially affect MT dynamics (Ti et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites recent experimental evidence.

claim: The D417H and R262H mutations significantly promoted MT polymerization while not causing substantial changes within the MT lattice.
source: Interestingly, while these mutations were not seen to cause any substantial changes within the MT lattice, they significantly promoted MT polymerization.
evidence: This is based on the experimental observations of Ti et al., 2016.

claim: Ti et al., 2016 concluded that the D417H and R262H mutations might exploit an allosteric mechanism that reduces the fraction of kinked vs. straight tubulin dimers relative to wild-type tubulin.
source: Ti et al., 2016 have concluded that the mutations might exploit an allosteric mechanism that reduces the fraction of kinked vs. straight tubulin dimers relative to wild-type tubulin.
evidence: This cites the interpretation of experimental results by Ti et al., 2016.

claim: The β-tubulin mutation T238A known to yield hyperstable MTs in yeast has been shown to uncouple the conformational dynamics of tubulin from its GTP-hydrolyzing activity in MTs.
source: Another β-tubulin mutation (T238A) known to yield hyperstable MTs in yeast has been recently shown to uncouple the conformational dynamics of tubulin from its GTP-hydrolyzing activity in MTs (Machin et al., 1995; Geyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This cites experimental evidence.

claim: The T238A mutation reduces the propensity of tubulin dimers bound to the MT cap to be kinked.
source: The authors demonstrated that this mutation also reduces the propensity of tubulin dimers bound to the MT cap to be kinked.
evidence: This is based on the experimental observations of Geyer et al., 2015.

claim: Multiple microsecond long MD simulations were performed of a tubulin dimer in solution in two different nucleotide states: GTP and GDP.
source: We have performed multiple microsecond long simulations of a tubulin dimer in solution in two different incarnations, GTP- and GDP-tubulin, and compared them to a set of all tubulin structures currently available in the Protein Data Bank (PDB).
evidence: This describes the computational methodology used in the study.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on a set of all tubulin structures currently deposited in the PDB.
source: In order to compare the simulated tubulin ensembles to experimentally known structures, we performed a principal component analysis (PCA) on a set of all tubulin structures currently deposited in the PDB (Figure 2, Figure 2—video 1; see also Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the analysis method used.

claim: No intermediate structures were observed in the known experimental data.
source: Interestingly, no intermediate structures were observed in the known experimental data, suggesting that the population of such intermediates is probably very low and may not be resolved by cryo-EM and X-ray crystallography.
evidence: This is an observation from the PCA analysis of experimental structures.

claim: The first conformational mode contributes ~90% to the total structural variation in the set and describes a dimer bending motion.
source: The first conformational mode contributes ∼90% to the total structural variation in the set and describes a dimer bending motion (Figure 2C, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is a result of the PCA analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Bending occurs around an 'anchor point' located at the intradimer interface that does not move during the transition.
source: Bending occurs around an 'anchor point' located at the intradimer interface that does not move during the transition. This anchor point involves hydrophobic interactions between the H8 helix of β-tubulin and the surface of α-tubulin.
evidence: This is observed from the PCA analysis and structural examination.

claim: The anchor point involves hydrophobic interactions between the H8 helix of β-tubulin and the surface of α-tubulin.
source: This anchor point involves hydrophobic interactions between the H8 helix of β-tubulin and the surface of α-tubulin.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the bending motion.

claim: A similar unaffected contact between adjacent dimers in MT protofilaments has been previously shown to be involved in MT lattice compaction upon GTP hydrolysis.
source: Interestingly, a similar unaffected contact, but between adjacent dimers in MT protofilaments, has been previously shown to be involved in MT lattice compaction upon GTP hydrolysis (Alushin et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This cites previous structural studies.

claim: The second conformational mode contributes ~5% to the total structural variation and describes a 'breathing' motion of the dimer.
source: The second conformational mode contributes ∼5% to the total structural variation and describes a 'breathing' motion of the dimer (Figure 2—video 3)
evidence: This is a result of the PCA analysis.

claim: The nucleotide state strongly affects tubulin bending flexibility.
source: Most importantly, the nucleotide state seemed to strongly affect tubulin bending flexibility.
evidence: This is observed from comparing the simulated ensembles of GTP- and GDP-tubulin in Figure 3.

claim: GDP-tubulin ensembles were on average more 'confined' during the simulation time.
source: While the GDP-tubulin ensembles were on average more 'confined' during the simulation time, GTP-tubulin was seen to explore a broader range of curvatures (Figure 3, motion along conformational mode 1)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 comparing the simulated ensembles.

claim: GTP-tubulin explores a broader range of curvatures than GDP-tubulin.
source: While the GDP-tubulin ensembles were on average more 'confined' during the simulation time, GTP-tubulin was seen to explore a broader range of curvatures (Figure 3, motion along conformational mode 1)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 comparing the simulated ensembles.

claim: The conformational change associated with the ensemble separation RC involves rearrangements in the individual monomers and at the intradimer interface.
source: A surprising result of this analysis is that the conformational change associated with the identified ensemble separation RC, indeed, was unrelated to tubulin bending or nucleotide state but rather involved rearrangements in the individual monomers and at the intradimer interface (Figure 4—video 1; discussed in detail in the last Results section).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and Figure 7A.

claim: The motion along the ensemble separation RC is uncoupled from the bending motion both for GTP- and GDP-tubulin.
source: Second, the motion along the ensemble separation RC is uncoupled from the bending motion both for GTP- and GDP-tubulin, confirming that the identified free energy barrier is unrelated to both tubulin curvature and nucleotide state.
evidence: This is shown in the 2D free energy profiles in Figure 4.

claim: Tubulin easily probes a wide range of curvatures independently of the starting conformation.
source: Finally, it can be inferred from these 2D profiles that, in our simulations, tubulin easily probes a wide range of curvatures (motion along the y-axis), independently of the starting conformation and with GDP-tubulin sampling a much more restricted range of curvatures (Figure 4, left vs. right panel).
evidence: This is inferred from the 2D free energy profiles in Figure 4.

claim: Two different bending modes exist: the splay-bend (SB) and twist-bend (TB) mode.
source: To distinguish between these two different motions later on, we refer to them as the splay-bend (SB) and twist-bend (TB) mode, respectively.
evidence: This is based on the functional mode analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: GTP-tubulin favors a much broader range of intrinsic curvatures, all of which are almost isoenergetic (free energy differences of 1−2 kT).
source: Comparison of the free energy profiles for GTP- and GDP-tubulin revealed that GTP-tubulin favors a much broader range of intrinsic curvatures, all of which are almost isoenergetic (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1; free energy differences of 1−2 kT).
evidence: This is shown in the free energy profiles in Figure 6.

claim: GTP does not shift the bending preference of tubulin toward low-curvature states.
source: Contrary to what is postulated by the allosteric model, GTP does not shift the bending preference of tubulin toward low-curvature states according to our calculations.
evidence: This is based on the free energy profiles in Figure 6 which show that GTP-tubulin does not favor straight conformations.

claim: The range of curvatures energetically accessible to GDP-tubulin becomes strongly restrained (steeper free energy curves).
source: Rather, the range of curvatures energetically accessible to GDP-tubulin becomes strongly restrained (steeper free energy curves in Figure 6)
evidence: This is shown in the free energy profiles in Figure 6.

claim: Intermediate dimer kinking is preserved in either nucleotide state.
source: while intermediate dimer kinking is preserved in either nucleotide state (approximate coincidence of the free energy minima in Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in the free energy profiles in Figure 6.

claim: Tubulin might gain considerable flexibility through binding GTP without changing its average, intermediately kinked conformation.
source: This suggests that tubulin might gain considerable flexibility through binding GTP without changing its average, intermediately kinked conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the free energy profiles in Figure 6.

claim: Visual inspection of the ensemble separation RC revealed several large-amplitude internal rearrangements in the α- and β-tubulin monomers including an upward-downward movement of the central H7 helix accompanied by a translocation of the H7-H8 loop.
source: Visual inspection of the respective collective motion (Figure 7A and Figure 4—video 1) revealed several large-amplitude internal rearrangements in the α- and β-tubulin monomers that might contribute to the observed barrier. Those include an upward-downward movement of the central H7 helix in the intermediate domain (residues 206–371) accompanied by a translocation of the H7-H8 loop, which leads to a shift in the position of the anchor point
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The rearrangements lead to a shift in the position of the anchor point.
source: Those include an upward-downward movement of the central H7 helix in the intermediate domain (residues 206–371) accompanied by a translocation of the H7-H8 loop, which leads to a shift in the position of the anchor point
evidence: This is observed from the structural analysis of the ensemble separation RC.

claim: Crossing the barrier along the ensemble separation RC does not require the dimer to bend but rather induces changes in the monomer structure and at the intradimer interface.
source: Hence, crossing the barrier along the ensemble separation RC does not require the dimer to bend but rather induces changes in the monomer structure and at the intradimer interface.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis of the ensemble separation RC.

claim: The results suggest a new mechanism by which GTP binding by unassembled tubulin is linked to its conformational dynamics.
source: Our results suggest a new mechanism by which GTP binding by unassembled tubulin is linked to its conformational dynamics.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the simulation results.

claim: The new mechanism reconciles the previously proposed lattice and allosteric models into a new unified model.
source: This mechanism reconciles the previously proposed lattice and allosteric models (Figure 1) into a new unified model, hence resolving the discrepancies between previous experimental observations.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: In solution, tubulin can exist in two anchor point states, each capable of nucleotide-dependent bending but differing in the way the dimer bends.
source: We propose that tubulin enters the MT lattice via a combination of both mechanisms (Figure 8). In solution, tubulin can exist in two anchor point states, each capable of nucleotide-dependent bending but differing in the way the dimer bends, with the SB bending mode being strongly energetically favored over the TB mode
evidence: This is the proposed model based on the simulation results.

claim: The SB bending mode is strongly energetically favored over the TB mode.
source: In solution, tubulin can exist in two anchor point states, each capable of nucleotide-dependent bending but differing in the way the dimer bends, with the SB bending mode being strongly energetically favored over the TB mode (Figure 4; Figure 7B; Figure 8, horizontal transition in the bottom cycle).
evidence: This is based on the free energy calculations shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The average dimer conformation in either anchor point state is intermediately kinked, irrespective of the bound nucleotide.
source: The average dimer conformation in either state is intermediately kinked, irrespective of the bound nucleotide (Figure 6)
evidence: This is based on the free energy profiles in Figure 6.

claim: The average intermediately kinked conformation might explain experimental observations that colchicine binding and SAXS profiles of soluble GTP- and GDP-tubulin are almost identical.
source: The average dimer conformation in either state is intermediately kinked, irrespective of the bound nucleotide (Figure 6), which might explain experimental observations that colchicine binding and SAXS profiles of soluble GTP- and GDP-tubulin are almost identical (Manuel Andreu et al., 1989; Rice et al., 2008).
evidence: This connects the simulation results to previous experimental observations.

claim: The findings are consistent with early dimer and follow-up protofilament simulations where both dimers and protofilaments (GTP and GDP) attained largely kinked conformations on the several tens of nanoseconds timescale.
source: In this respect, our findings are also consistent with the early dimer (Gebremichael et al., 2008) and follow-up protofilament simulations (Grafmüller and Voth, 2011; Grafmüller et al., 2013) where both dimers and protofilaments (GTP and GDP) attained largely kinked conformations on the several tens of nanoseconds timescale.
evidence: This compares the current results with previous computational studies.

claim: Bending flexibility at the intradimer interface is controlled by the nucleotide state and gets strongly enhanced upon GTP binding.
source: We have now shown that bending flexibility at the intradimer interface is controlled by the nucleotide state and gets strongly enhanced upon GTP binding (Figure 6; Figure 8, upward transition in the bottom cycle).
evidence: This is based on the free energy profiles in Figure 6.

claim: Allosteric control through GTP binding differs conceptually from that proposed by the canonical allosteric model, wherein GTP binding forces tubulin to undergo a kinked-to-straight conformational change.
source: Although allosteric control through GTP binding is still present in our model, it differs conceptually from that proposed by the canonical allosteric model (Figure 1, right branch), wherein GTP binding forces tubulin to undergo a kinked-to-straight conformational change.
evidence: This contrasts the proposed model with the canonical allosteric model.

claim: The GTP-induced increase in flexibility does not force tubulin to adopt the straight MT-like conformation, which is in part compatible with the lattice model.
source: In our model, the GTP-induced increase in flexibility does not force tubulin to adopt the straight MT-like conformation, which is in part compatible with the lattice model (Figure 1, left branch).
evidence: This relates the proposed model to the lattice model.

claim: Straightening of kinked tubulin at the MT tip and within the lattice is accomplished through induced fit.
source: Straightening of kinked tubulin at the MT tip and within the lattice is accomplished through induced fit, i.e. the energy of kinking stress (Figure 6, left) is compensated by lateral and longitudinal bond energies.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The energy of kinking stress is compensated by lateral and longitudinal bond energies.
source: Straightening of kinked tubulin at the MT tip and within the lattice is accomplished through induced fit, i.e. the energy of kinking stress (Figure 6, left) is compensated by lateral and longitudinal bond energies.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The straightening scenario is merely a lattice effect and does not involve allosteric regulation via GTP.
source: This compensation is merely a lattice effect and does not involve allosteric regulation via GTP.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The scenario does not contradict experimental data where MTs polymerized with GMPCPP were seen to depolymerize into significantly less curved protofilaments than normal MTs.
source: Notably, this scenario does not contradict the experimental data where MTs polymerized with a non-hydrolyzable GTP-analog, GMPCPP, were seen to depolymerize into significantly less curved protofilaments than normal MTs (Müller-Reichert et al., 1998)
evidence: This relates the proposed model to experimental observations.

claim: Intermediate-curvature states of polymers made of GMPCPP-tubulin were observed by cryo-EM.
source: and intermediate-curvature states of polymers made of GMPCPP-tubulin were observed by cryo-EM (Wang and Nogales, 2005; Nogales and Wang, 2006).
evidence: This cites experimental observations.

claim: Formation of straight or less kinked GTP-tubulin conformations at MT tips might not strictly require that those conformations be energetically favored in solution.
source: Formation of straight or less kinked GTP-tubulin conformations at MT tips, we think, might not strictly require that those conformations be energetically favored in solution.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the proposed model.

claim: Less kinked, cap-bound GTP-dimers would be more likely to be observed, given at least one lateral neighbor.
source: Less kinked, cap-bound GTP-dimers would be more likely to be observed, given at least one lateral neighbor.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the proposed model.

claim: The coexistence of two curvature- and nucleotide-independent anchor point states separated by a large free energy barrier is striking.
source: The coexistence of the two curvature- and nucleotide-independent anchor point states separated by a large free energy barrier is striking (Figure 4; Figure 7).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results.

claim: One possibility is that the activation energy to cross the SB-TB barrier for a newly arrived dimer at the MT tip comes from favorable lateral and longitudinal bond formation.
source: The first possibility is sketched in Figure 8 (top cycle) and assumes that the activation energy to cross the SB-TB barrier for a newly arrived dimer at the MT tip comes from favorable lateral and longitudinal bond formation.
evidence: This is a speculation about how the barrier might be overcome.

claim: The second possibility is that SB and TB dimers are equally well incorporated into the MT lattice, and that the transition may be accomplished much later in the MT body.
source: The second possibility is that SB and TB dimers are equally well incorporated into the MT lattice, and that the transition may be accomplished much later in the MT body.
evidence: This is an alternative speculation about how the barrier might be overcome.

claim: The first possibility is favored because no tubulin structure derived from the MT body has (yet) been deposited showing a dimer in the SB state.
source: While we cannot discriminate between the two possibilities at present, we favor the first because: (a) no tubulin structure derived from the MT body has (yet) been deposited showing a dimer in the SB state
evidence: This is based on the absence of experimental structures showing SB dimers in the MT body.

claim: The values for longitudinal and lateral bond energies found in literature seem to be sufficient to antagonize the high SB-TB barrier.
source: and (b) the values for longitudinal and lateral bond energies found in literature seem to be sufficient to antagonize the high SB-TB barrier (VanBuren et al., 2002; VanBuren et al., 2005; Gardner et al., 2011; Castle and Odde, 2013; Kononova et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on literature values for bond energies.

claim: The longitudinal bond energy ranges between −16.8 kT and −25.2 kT (not including the entropic cost of binding from the bulk to the MT tip which is ~10 kT).
source: More specifically, the longitudinal bond energy ranges between −16.8 kT and −25.2 kT (not including the entropic cost of binding from the bulk to the MT tip which is ∼10 kT([Castle and Odde, 2013))
evidence: This cites literature values for longitudinal bond energy.

claim: The lateral bond energy is estimated to be between −3.6 kT and −11.7 kT.
source: while the lateral bond energy is estimated to be between −3.6 kT and −11.7 kT.
evidence: This cites literature values for lateral bond energy.

claim: Taking the lower bounds of the bond energy estimates, one arrives at a combined (one lateral and one longitudinal) energy of −20.4 kT, which is already enough to counterbalance the high SB-TB activation energy.
source: Taking the lower bounds of these estimates, one arrives at a combined (one lateral and one longitudinal) energy of −20.4 kT, which is already enough to counterbalance the high SB-TB activation energy.
evidence: This is a calculation based on literature values.

claim: The barrier separating the two anchor point states, in addition to the nucleotide state, may control the kinetics of MT assembly and disassembly, i.e. MT catastrophe rates.
source: Although we cannot provide strong evidence for the functional role of the barrier separating the two anchor point states (Figure 7), it is tempting to speculate that this barrier, in addition to the nucleotide state, may control the kinetics of MT assembly and disassembly, i.e. MT catastrophe rates.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional role of the barrier.

claim: Modern mechanochemical computational models of MT assembly are unable to reproduce typical MT lifetimes (several minutes), lengths (several microns), as well as their moderate dependence on free tubulin concentration observed in vitro.
source: In fact, this barrier might resolve the so far unexplained inability of modern mechanochemical computational models of MT assembly (VanBuren et al., 2002; VanBuren et al., 2005; Margolin et al., 2011; Margolin et al., 2012; Castle and Odde, 2013; Zakharov et al., 2015) to reproduce typical MT lifetimes (several minutes), lengths (several microns), as well as their moderate dependence on free tubulin concentration observed in vitro (Walker et al., 1988; Walker et al., 1991; Gardner et al., 2011)
evidence: This cites limitations of previous computational models.

claim: The dependence of MT lifetimes and lengths on free tubulin concentration is predicted to be too steep by current models.
source: This dependence of MT lifetimes and lengths on free tubulin concentration is predicted to be too steep (VanBuren et al., 2002)
evidence: This cites a limitation of previous computational models.

claim: Current models predict a characteristic time for a catastrophe event under physiologically relevant concentrations being on the order of years.
source: implying a characteristic time for a catastrophe event under physiologically relevant concentrations being on the order of years (Zakharov et al., 2015).
evidence: This cites a limitation of previous computational models.

claim: There must be a lack of important mechanical features which causes a 'hyperstabilization' of the MT in current models.
source: There must be therefore a lack of important mechanical features which causes a 'hyperstabilization' of the MT in these models.
evidence: This is inferred from the limitations of current models.

claim: The results obtained with atomistic MD simulations may provide some of the missing features in current mechanochemical models.
source: Our results obtained with atomistic MD simulations may now provide some of these missing features.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential impact of the current results.

claim: The new combined model of MT assembly cross-bridges previous contradictory experimental observations.
source: In conclusion, our results, combined with previous structural knowledge, extend our understanding of MT dynamic instability. In particular, the new combined model of MT assembly cross-bridges previous contradictory experimental observations
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Assuming that GTP-induced tubulin flexibility, and not the dimer conformation as such, is the driving force for MT assembly resolves the discrepancy between previous models and reconciles contradictory experimental data.
